entries.title: Judging any seal on any package
entries.question: How do I know if a seal on a package means anything?
entries.decision: A named outside group’s seal over a company badge.
entries.why: A badge a company gave itself has neither. Each real seal covers one scope.
entries.short_answer: Ask three questions of any seal. Who set the standard? Is it published? Does an independent body audit against it? A company’s own badge answers none of them. No seal covers what it never set out to measure.
entries.detail: The gap between a certification and a marketing badge is entirely in the audit. Real programs publish their standard, so anyone can read exactly what was checked, and they send inspectors. The second half of reading a seal is scope: an organic seal covers inputs and practices and says nothing about welfare beyond a baseline, a welfare seal says nothing about pesticides, and a non-GMO seal addresses one issue only. Stacking seals on a package does not make it a better food, it makes it a food that paid for several audits. The ingredient panel still decides what the thing actually is. A badge a company created for its own products answers none of the three questions. USDA Organic, Real Organic Project, Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, Global Animal Partnership and the Non-GMO Project all publish standards and use outside auditors. Real Organic Project sits on top of the organic seal and requires soil-grown crops and pastured animals. A farm that sells direct, where the grower answers questions about sprays, feed and pasture, reaches past what any seal audits. What no seal tells you is anything it never set out to measure.
sources: Real Organic Project: Standards
7 CFR 205 organic certification requirements (label meaning)
Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved and Global Animal Partnership published standards
Non-GMO Project verification standard
entries.kristy_take: A badge a company gave itself is a sticker. The real ones publish, and they inspect.
buying_tips: A named program you can look up, not a decorative badge the company gave itself.

entries.title: ‘Cold-pressed’, ‘expeller-pressed’, ‘refined’
entries.question: What do ‘cold-pressed’ and ‘expeller-pressed’ mean on an oil?
entries.decision: Cold-pressed or expeller-pressed olive or coconut oil, unrefined.
entries.why: Organic handling rules bar volatile synthetic solvents as processing aids.
entries.short_answer: Expeller-pressed means a mechanical screw press with no solvent, though friction still generates heat. Cold-pressed is the same press with the temperature held down. Most supermarket cooking oil is neither. It is solvent-extracted, then refined, bleached and deodorized.
entries.detail: Extraction and refining are two separate steps and both matter. Mechanical pressing leaves more of the original flavor, color and aroma in the oil, which is exactly why unrefined oils taste like the thing they came from and refined ones taste like nothing. Solvent extraction pulls far more oil out of the same seed, which is why it dominates at commercial scale. In the US ‘cold-pressed’ has no federal definition for most oils, so it carries less weight on a sunflower bottle than on an olive one. But the press only sorts oils that already clear the bar. Which oil it is settles the purchase first, and the pressing decides between two good ones after that. Two of these words describe pressing and one describes what happens afterwards. For olive oil in the EU, cold-pressed is a defined temperature limit. “Pure” and “refined” both describe oil stripped of color, flavor and aroma.

sources.name: Dr. Cate Shanahan: The Hateful Eight seed oils

entries.kristy_take: Pressed oil tastes like what it came from. Refined oil tastes like nothing, on purpose.

entries.title: ‘Sugar-free’ and what replaced the sugar
entries.question: If it says sugar-free, what is doing the sweetening?
entries.decision: Unsweetened food, with no sugar substitutes listed.
entries.why: ‘Sugar-free’ is a defined claim about what came out. The list names what went in.
entries.short_answer: Something else, named on the ingredient list. ‘Sugar-free’ is defined as under half a gram of sugar per serving. The sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol or a high-intensity sweetener. ‘Unsweetened’ generally means nothing sweet was added at all.
entries.detail: ‘Sugar-free’ answers a Nutrition Facts question and says nothing about what took sugar’s place, which is why the ingredient list matters more here than on almost any other claim. Sugar alcohols appear by name and are also totalled on the panel; high-intensity sweeteners appear in the list and are used in tiny amounts. ‘Unsweetened’ has no formal FDA definition and in practice means no sweetener of any kind, including the non-caloric ones, which makes it the cleaner word to look for on yogurt, plant milk and apple sauce. ‘Naturally sweetened’ has no definition at all and covers honey, maple syrup and juice concentrate. Under ‘sugar-free’, the sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol (erythritol, maltitol, xylitol) or a high-intensity sweetener (stevia, monk fruit, sucralose, aspartame). ‘Unsweetened’ is the plainer word, and the two are not interchangeable.

entries.title: Seafood labels: wild, farm-raised, origin
entries.question: What has to be on a seafood label?
entries.decision: Wild fish with an MSC label, country and catch method on the tag.
entries.why: Wild is the seafood premise; the production-method label distinguishes wild from farm-raised fish.
entries.short_answer: Most unprocessed fish and shellfish at retail must show the species, wild-caught or farm-raised, and the country of origin. Federal country-of-origin labeling requires it. The catch: origin can mean where it was processed, not where it was caught.
entries.detail: Country-of-origin labeling covers unprocessed fish and shellfish and is genuinely useful, since it turns ‘farm-raised, product of ___‘ into a readable pair rather than a guess. Two limits are worth knowing. Cooked, breaded or otherwise processed seafood falls outside the rule. And species naming has a long history of substitution, where one fish is sold under another species name, which is a far bigger problem on a bare fillet than on a whole fish or a piece with the skin left on. Buying whole, buying skin-on, and buying from a counter that can answer the origin question are the practical defenses. Country-of-origin labeling is one of the few places a store must tell you where food came from.
entries.kristy_take: Species, method, country. Then buy it skin-on, because the species name is the one that gets swapped.
buying_tips: Read the tag for “wild-caught” or “farm-raised”, the country, and the catch method.
Wild-caught salmon over farm-raised.
Whole or skin-on fish, far harder to swap than a bare fillet.
Can’t find wild salmon: farm-raised, with the country of origin read.

entries.title: Serving size and the numbers under it
entries.question: Why do the numbers on the panel look so low?
entries.decision: Whole foods; compare labels at equal grams per serving.
entries.why: Every number is per serving. Half of what looks reasonable is a third of the package.
entries.short_answer: Because every number on the Nutrition Facts panel is per serving. The servings-per-container line says how many the package holds. ‘About 2.5 servings’ means multiplying everything by two and a half. Serving sizes reflect what people typically eat.
entries.detail: This is the easiest number on a package to misread, and it is not an accident that it sits at the top in small type. The reference amounts are fixed by the FDA per food category, so competing products in the same category are genuinely comparable, which is the useful thing about them. What they are not is a recommendation. The 2016 label rules made serving sizes more realistic, put added sugars on their own line, and required dual-column labelling on packages that could plausibly be finished in one sitting. Read from the top down: servings per container first, serving size second, then the numbers. Serving sizes are set by regulation to reflect what people typically eat, not what is good for anyone, and larger single-serve packages now have to show a per-package column too.
sources: FDA Nutrition Facts label final rule (2016)
FDA Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed, 21 CFR 101.12

entries.title: “Artificial color” and what it need not name
entries.question: What does “artificial color” mean on an ingredient list?
entries.decision: Food with no added coloring on the list.
entries.why: Certified dyes must be named; others, titanium dioxide among them, may hide under a group term.
entries.short_answer: “Red 40” always appears by name; a group term need not say which color.
entries.detail: The split is written into 21 CFR 101.22(k). Paragraph (k)(1) requires each color additive subject to certification to be declared by the name in its own regulation, dropping the “FD&C” prefix but keeping “Lake” where it applies. Paragraph (k)(2) lets colors not subject to certification use the collective terms “Artificial Color,” “Artificial Color Added” or “Color Added,” or “Colored with ______,” which names the substance. Titanium dioxide, listed at 21 CFR 73.575, is exempt from certification and capped at one percent of the food by weight; it is the white pigment for opacity in candy shells, frosting, chewing gum and creamy dressings. The EU removed it from food after a review by its food safety authority, and food makers there took it out. Where a panel reads “artificial color” with no number beside it, the color is one federal rules did not require to be named, and the panel alone cannot say which. The plain move at the shelf is a list with no added color, or a color named from a food.
sources: Food Babe: 3 ingredients to check for (titanium dioxide under “artificial color” or “color added”)
Chris Kresser: Why you should know how to read a nutrition label (colors under umbrella terms)
21 CFR 101.22(k) declaration of color additives on the ingredient list (label meaning)
21 CFR 73.575 titanium dioxide: one percent limit, exempt from certification (label meaning)
entries.kristy_take: Named colors had to name themselves. The collective phrase covers the ones that did not. So “artificial color” stands where an ingredient would be: legal, complete, and vaguer than it looks.

Can’t find it: one colored with a named food.

entries.science: Certified dyes must be declared by name; colors exempt from certification may be declared as a group. Titanium dioxide is a white pigment exempt from certification. A label may name it outright, though nothing requires that.

entries.title: Raw kefir
entries.question: Is raw kefir worth buying?
entries.decision: Plain raw or grass-fed kefir from whole milk, Certified Grassfed, farm named.
entries.why: A live ferment from a named herd. The refrigerated case is the only place it exists.
entries.card_why: Kefir is what a dairy does with milk it wants to keep, and it has been doing it for centuries. The grains turn it tangy and thick and it holds for weeks where the milk holds for days. The rule is the milk’s rule: the farm is the product. Buy it from the herd you would drink from raw, as close to the culture date as the case allows.
entries.short_answer: Raw kefir is a live ferment and it has to be sold cold. Anything shelf-stable was heat-treated after culturing, which ends the thing you were buying it for.
entries.detail: Kefir carries a wider mix of cultures than yogurt and pours rather than spoons. Made from raw milk it is the same sourcing question as the milk: a named farm, a small herd, a cold chain. Plain is the only version worth buying. The flavored tubs carry the added sugar of a dessert and the ferment becomes the excuse.
entries.kristy_take: Same farm as the milk, or it is just a drink.
buying_tips: ‘raw’ and a farm name on the bottle, the same farm as the milk.

Commercial bottles taste different because of what was added. Flavoring, additives and sugar make the difference, so plain is the one where the ferment is what you taste.

entries.title: Raw aged cheese
entries.question: Is raw milk cheese worth buying?
entries.decision: Grass-fed raw-milk cheese, aged 60 days or more.
entries.why: Aged raw-milk cheese tastes of one herd and season, and its maker has to know the milk.
entries.card_why: Aged raw-milk cheese is the raw dairy nobody has to hunt for. US rules allow it at sixty days and up, so a decent cheese counter already keeps a case of it. Sixty days of aging is a technology of its own. It is the reason an aged raw cheddar tastes of the place it came from. A young commodity block tastes of very little. The organizing principle is the milk’s: ask who made it, from which herd, and how long it sat.
entries.short_answer: It is the raw dairy nobody has to go looking for. US law lets raw-milk cheese aged sixty days or more sell across state lines. It sits in ordinary cheese cases. Most traditional European cheeses are made this way.
entries.detail: The sixty-day rule is why raw cheese is legal at US retail where raw milk often is not. Aging concentrates the cheese and develops it, and a raw-milk cheese carries the character of one herd and one season in a way a standardized pasteurized curd is designed not to. A staffed counter can usually name the maker, the animal and the age, which is exactly the information the rind label is too small to hold. Raw-milk cheese sits in the case beside everything else: no farm visit, no herdshare, no state-by-state map. Most traditional European cheeses are made this way, which is why so many qualify.
entries.kristy_take: Ask the monger who made it. A good one has been waiting to tell you.
buying_tips: ‘raw milk’ or ‘lait cru’ (French for raw milk) with an age on the label.
A named maker and a named herd, not just a country.

entries.title: Sprouts
entries.question: Are sprouts worth buying?
entries.decision: Crisp organic broccoli, radish or mung sprouts, kept cold.
entries.why: Sprouts are eaten whole and raw, and organic rules bar synthetic substances and GMOs in growing.
entries.card_why: Sprouts are about as alive as produce gets, a seed caught mid-decision, sold days old. That is the appeal, and it is also the whole handling question. The warm damp days that sprout a seed are the same days that sprout everything else. A grower who keeps them cold from the sprouting room to the case is doing the only thing that matters. Past that, a jar and a screen on your own counter costs almost nothing. It puts the sourcing question entirely in your hands.
entries.short_answer: Yes, chosen well. Broccoli, radish or mung from the cold case, with white roots and no sour smell. Home-grown from organic seed works too. Skip alfalfa and soy sprouts. Weston A. Price guidance eats them lightly steamed, not raw.
entries.detail: Weston A. Price Foundation guidance accepts organic sprouting seeds with two exceptions, alfalfa and soybean. Alfalfa seeds contain canavanine, and raw sprouts hold irritants that are neutralized in cooking, so the guidance is to eat them lightly steamed or cooked. Sprouting has been a winter green in kitchens for a very long time, and a jar with a mesh lid on the counter still produces a crop in three or four days. Buying them is fine when the case is cold and turnover is quick; sprouts go slick and sour before they look wrong.
entries.kristy_take: A jar, a mesh lid and organic seed grow a crop at home. Bought sprouts come from the cold case; steam them lightly before eating.

entries.title: Root vegetables: carrots, potatoes, beets
entries.question: How do I choose and store carrots, potatoes, sweet potatoes, and beets?
entries.decision: Firm organic carrots, potatoes and beets, with no sprouts.
entries.why: Roots grow in the soil and the skin often gets eaten, so how they were grown comes first.
entries.short_answer: Firm is the test at every root. Potatoes: no bruises, nicks or soft spots, never green. Carrots: well colored, no green shoulders, wilt, flab or cracks. Sweet potatoes: smooth, even shape, even peel color. Beets: round, slender tap root.
entries.detail: Top tier is in season with a Real Organic, Certified Naturally Grown, Demeter or Regenerative Organic Certified seal, then USDA Organic as the floor; read the sign or sticker at the bin for the growing method. Potatoes keep up to a month in a cool, dark place with good ventilation, ideally 45 to 50°F. Throw away any that turn shriveled or green or grow many sprouts. Sweet potatoes want cool and dry, 55 to 59°F: colder brings chilling injury (fungal decay, internal browning, shriveling) and warmer speeds sprouting. Carrots go in a closed bag or container in the refrigerator for up to two weeks. Cut the tops off first, since attached tops wilt the root, and a wilted carrot revives in a soak of cold water. Beets: trim the leafy stem to an inch, leave the root end on, and refrigerate in a food-safe container for up to two weeks. Stored potatoes are often treated with a sprout inhibitor, so fresh-dug local potatoes come first.
sources: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping Guide Categories
Weston A. Price Foundation: Extend to the End, Prolonging Your Local Growing Season
Organic Federation of Canada: Organic sprout inhibitors for potatoes caught in red tape
entries.kristy_take: Wilted beet leaves need not put you off a firm root. Cut the tops off carrots before storing them; left attached, they wilt the carrot.
buying_tips: Look for Real Organic Project on the sign: grown in soil, never hydroponic.
No Real Organic or Certified Naturally Grown logo: plain organic, which still allows approved sprays.

entries.question: How do I pick fresh broccoli, cauliflower, or cabbage?
entries.decision: Tight broccoli, cabbage and cauliflower, heavy for their size.
entries.why: Tight, dark green broccoli florets are fresh. Enlarged, open or yellowish-green ones are past fresh.
entries.short_answer: Broccoli: dark green florets, closed, not yellowish or wilted, on stems that are not thick and tough. Cauliflower: no bruises or damage. Cabbage: strip wilted or insect-damaged outer leaves. A soft or slippery head stays on the shelf.
entries.detail: Top tier is in season with a Real Organic, Certified Naturally Grown, Demeter or Regenerative Organic Certified seal, then USDA Organic as the floor; read the sign or sticker at the bin for the growing method. Broccoli is the short keeper of the three: refrigerate it in a plastic bag with holes and use it within three days. Cabbage goes the other way, staying fresh for several weeks in a plastic bag or wrap in the refrigerator at 41°F or below; before using, cut out the core and rinse the leaves under cool running water. Cauliflower gets kept away from raw meat and meat juices.
sources: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping Guide Categories
Weston A. Price Foundation: Extend to the End, Prolonging Your Local Growing Season
entries.kristy_take: A soft or slippery head is spoiling. Use broccoli early in the week; it keeps about three days, while wrapped cabbage can wait several weeks in the fridge.

Browned florets on cauliflower: leave it and pick a creamy white head.
Soft or slippery anywhere on the head is a sign of spoilage. Leave it.
pick_steps: Broccoli, cabbage and cauliflower heavy for their size.
entries.science: Opened or yellowish-green florets mean broccoli past fresh; a soft, slippery head is already spoiling. Broccoli keeps three days, refrigerated in a bag with holes. Cabbage keeps several weeks wrapped in the refrigerator at 41°F or below. Remove its core and rinse the leaves before using. Keep cauliflower away from raw meat and meat juices.
entries.tier_note: Florets are eaten whole with no peel, so the grower comes first; cabbage sheds its outer leaves.

entries.title: Onions and garlic
entries.question: How do I pick onions and garlic that will keep?
entries.decision: Firm onions and garlic with dry, papery skins.
entries.why: A well-cured bulb feels dry at the neck and papery outside. A soft, scented or sprouting bulb is already on its way out.
entries.short_answer: Onions: firm for their size, little to no scent, a dry neck, no cuts, bruises or mold, no sprouting. Some loose skins are normal. Garlic: clean, white or true to the variety, well cured, cloves firm.
entries.detail: Onions and garlic are peeled, so a firm, dry, well-cured bulb is the standard and organic is a bonus. Whole dry onions live in a cool, dry, dark place with plenty of air movement: no plastic bags, no wrap, and not beside potatoes or anything else that releases moisture. Storage between 41 and 75°F favors sprouting, so the cooler the spot the better. Refrigeration is only for sweet or mild high-water varieties, on a low-humidity setting, and a cut onion goes in a sealed container for up to seven days. Garlic keeps one to two months at room temperature in low humidity before it softens, goes spongy, and shrivels from water loss; it sprouts fastest between 41 and 65°F, and its odor moves into other foods, so it gets stored on its own.
sources: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping Guide Categories
Weston A. Price Foundation: Extend to the End, Prolonging Your Local Growing Season
entries.kristy_take: A few loose onion skins are normal. Squeeze for firmness and little scent, then store whole onions where air can move, away from damp potatoes.

entries.title: Leafy greens: lettuce, spinach, kale
entries.question: How do I choose and keep lettuce, spinach, and kale?
entries.decision: Crisp organic lettuce, spinach and kale, kept cold.
entries.why: Spinach is highly perishable, and kale wilts in warmth. A leaf that still stands crisp tells you it has freshness left.
entries.short_answer: Lettuce: crisp, green outside, pale at the heart. Romaine: neither very loose nor very hard. Spinach: uniformly green and fully crisp. Kale: firm, deep colored leaves on moist, hardy stems.
entries.detail: Cold is the whole storage story. Romaine keeps about 21 days near 32°F and noticeably less at 41°F, so the coldest shelf of the refrigerator is the right one. Spinach wants 32°F too and will not hold good quality past two weeks; at 41 to 50°F it wilts and yellows faster. Kale goes in a plastic bag with as much air pressed out as possible, unwashed, for about five days; water on the leaves speeds spoilage, so wash at the point of use. Small greenhouse growers sell living lettuce with the root ball on; one says the root ball doubles the shelf life, and another packs it to stay fresh up to three weeks. Greenhouse or hydroponic alone does not say how it was grown, so look for a Real Organic, Certified Naturally Grown, Demeter or Regenerative Organic Certified seal, then USDA Organic. In a big store, organic spring mix and romaine are the fallback. At the shelf, lettuce runs bright to dark green outside and yellow or light green at the heart, free of insects, decay, or damage. A very loose romaine head is immature; a very firm or hard one is overmature. Spinach should be fairly clean with no serious damage. Kale should show no browning, yellow, or small holes.

entries.title: Bell peppers
entries.question: How do I choose and keep bell peppers?
entries.decision: Firm, even organic bell peppers, glossy and unwrinkled.
entries.why: The pepper wall and skin are eaten, and organic rules bar synthetic substances and GMOs in growing.
entries.short_answer: Green peppers: judged on size, firmness, and color. Colored peppers: at least half colored, firm, and uniform in shape and size. Skip any with cracks, decay, sunburn, disease, insect damage, or bruises.
entries.detail: Peppers keep best around 45°F, three to five weeks, and shrivel from water loss when stored warmer. At 41°F they hold about two weeks before chilling injury begins to show as pitting, decay, softening, or a discolored seed cavity; red and other colored peppers are less sensitive to chilling than green ones. Keep peppers away from raw meat and meat juices. A dark, sunken spot at the blossom end is blossom end rot.
entries.kristy_take: Red, yellow and orange peppers tolerate cold better than green ones. In a fridge at 41°F, plan on about two weeks; leave any cracked or bruised pepper at the bin.

entries.title: Apples and pears
entries.question: How do I choose and keep apples and pears?
entries.decision: Organic apples and pears, firm, unbruised and unwaxed.
entries.why: Apples should feel crisp. A firm green Bartlett pear can ripen at home, turning sweet, juicy and buttery.
entries.short_answer: Apples: firm and crisp, not mealy, free of bruising, decay, cracks, and insect injury. Pears: sound shape and size, free of bruising, insect damage, and decay. A firm green Bartlett is not a fault.
entries.detail: Cold and dark is the storage rule: 30 to 32°F is best and up to 40°F still works, in a ventilated box or a plastic bag with holes, unwashed, since the moisture from washing hastens decay. Gala apples soften quickly, so cool them fast; McIntosh and Honeycrisp are prone to chilling injury and want 38°F. Refrigerated apples keep up to a month. Keep apples and pears away from raw meat and meat juices. Added edible coatings sit on the Weston A. Price Foundation avoid list, and orchards that skip synthetic sprays and wax coatings say so, so ask at the stand: waxed or coated? On apples, look for cracks at the stem or blossom end. Bartletts are picked mature-green and ripened off the tree; a ripe one is sweet, aromatic, and juicy with a buttery texture.

entries.title: Citrus: oranges, lemons, limes
entries.question: How do I choose and keep oranges, lemons, and limes?
entries.decision: Firm, smooth citrus; untreated and unwaxed when using the zest.
entries.why: Yellow limes carry more juice. A partly green orange can be fully mature, so feel for a firm, smooth rind.
entries.short_answer: Oranges: even color, firm, smooth, free of decay and bruising. A partly green orange can be fully mature. Lemons: even yellow, smooth, firm, no shriveling. Limes: firm and smooth, no dryness.
entries.detail: Oranges keep at room temperature for up to a week and in the refrigerator for up to three weeks. Lemons hold best around 54 to 57°F and limes around 50 to 55°F, warmer than a refrigerator. A lemon or lime that has turned yellow is the one to use first: lemons picked fully yellow and limes picked yellow must be marketed quickly, while the fruit picked dark green keeps longest. At the bin, oranges should show even, intense color, free of skin blemishes and discoloration. A partly green orange gets its color from degreening, which does not change the inside. Lemons should be free of decay, drying, and rind stains. Green limes are preferred in the US, but yellow limes carry more juice; pick limes free of bruises and oil spotting. Conventional citrus is often treated after harvest with imazalil or thiabendazole fungicides, and residues are measurable in the peel, so organic or untreated is the pick, most of all when the zest goes in.

entries.title: Stone fruit: peaches, nectarines, plums, cherries
entries.question: How do I choose and keep peaches, nectarines, plums, and cherries?
entries.decision: Organic peaches, nectarines and cherries, plump with stems on.
entries.why: A peach’s green background turns yellow as it readies. Unbruised fruit is the pick.
entries.short_answer: Peaches and nectarines: ground color turned from green to yellow. Plums: skin color turned for the variety. Cherries: at least light red all over, with green fleshy stems.
entries.detail: The optimum storage for all of them is just above freezing, 30.5 to 32°F, and Michigan Fresh puts cherries in the refrigerator at or below 41°F. Plums held between 36 and 46°F, the killing range, are more susceptible to internal breakdown: mealiness, browning, and failure to ripen. Peaches, nectarines, and plums picked well mature ripen on their own without ethylene; ethylene does not speed cherry ripening. Keep stone fruit away from raw meat and meat juices. On EWG’s Dirty Dozen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, both peaches and cherries appear. A peach or nectarine with a flesh firmness of 2 to 3 pounds-force counts as ready to eat, and the same holds for plums. Dark skin staining is inking, a cosmetic mark from abrasion that affects the skin only. Cherries should be at least light red across the whole surface, with no cracks, bird pecks, shriveling, or decay; green, fleshy stems go with freshness.

entries.decision: Grain labeled ‘sprouted whole’, the grain named as whole.

The whole grain claimed on a package is its dry weight, after the sprouting water is subtracted. A refined grain cannot sprout, because the sprout comes from the germ. entries.title: Gluten-free bread
entries.question: How do you pick gluten-free bread?
entries.decision: Gluten-free sourdough or sprouted bread, a whole-grain flour first.
entries.why: “Whole” in the first ingredient suggests a mostly whole-grain product; the wording is not a guarantee.
entries.short_answer: “Gluten-free”, “no gluten”, “free of gluten” and “without gluten” all meet one federal limit. The claim is voluntary. Bakers replace gluten with blended flours and starches, plus a gum that binds the loaf.
entries.detail: All four claim wordings mean the food has less than 20 ppm (parts per million) gluten under one federal labeling rule. Wheat starch may appear only if the food stays under 20 ppm. The claim is voluntary. Bakers replace gluten with a blend of flours and starches, such as rice, potato or tapioca. A gum binder, usually xanthan gum or HPMC, mimics some of the stretch gluten gives. Gluten-free does not mean unrefined. Many gluten-free breads and mixes are mostly starch, with added sugar and gums. Grains were traditionally prepared by soaking, sprouting or leavening with wild yeast, and gluten-free sourdough and sprouted loaves follow that.

entries.decision: Whole-wheat sourdough or sprouted buns and rolls.
entries.why: Sourdough or sprouted whole grain is the traditional rung; whole wheat must be the only flour.
entries.short_answer: Sourdough or sprouted buns from organic whole grain are the top rung. Read the name on the bag. “Whole wheat” buns and rolls use whole wheat flour, no white flour. “Enriched buns” are made with enriched flour instead.
entries.detail: Buns and rolls are bread, so the bread tiers apply: sourdough, soaked or sprouted from organic whole grain flour on top, without added gluten, soy, bran or hydrogenated oils. One federal standard covers bread, rolls and buns. Under it, whole wheat buns, whole wheat rolls and graham buns are made from whole wheat flour, and no plain white flour is used. Enriched buns use enriched flour in place of some or all of the flour. A typical enriched hot dog bun lists enriched flour, water, yeast, sugar and soybean oil, a seed oil to skip.

entries.title: Pastries and bakery muffins
entries.question: Which fat is in a pastry or a bakery muffin?
entries.decision: Sprouted whole-grain muffins or sourdough pastries made with butter.
entries.why: Butter is the traditional fat in pastries and muffins. Factory-made versions often swap in other fats.
entries.short_answer: Read the fat and the sweetener, or ask the baker. The top rung is butter or coconut oil, a natural sweetener and soaked or sprouted whole grain flour. Skip shortening, hydrogenated oil and refined sugar or corn syrup.
entries.detail: On the traditional tiers, the best muffins and baked goods use organic natural sweeteners, soaked or sprouted whole grain flour, and butter, coconut oil or another traditional fat. Most commercial ones use partially hydrogenated oils and refined sweeteners such as sugar, high fructose corn syrup or agave. Danish pastry is laminated, meaning butter is folded into a yeast dough in thin layers. Butter is the traditional fat; industrial production often uses other fats, such as hydrogenated sunflower oil. The American muffin is a quick bread, raised by baking soda instead of yeast.

entries.title: Sour cream

entries.decision: Grass-fed sour cream, only cream and cultures.
entries.why: Grass-fed names the feeding standard; wAPF lists sour cream with additives, and homogenized cream, under avoid.
entries.short_answer: The tub names the method. Sour cream, or cultured sour cream, is cream soured by bacteria. Acidified sour cream is soured with added acids. Both hold at least 18 percent milkfat.
entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 131.160, sour cream is pasteurized cream soured by lactic acid bacteria. It may be named “Cultured sour cream”. Under 21 CFR 131.162, acidified sour cream is soured with acidifiers, with or without lactic acid bacteria. An acidifier is an added food-grade acid. Both hold at least 18 percent milkfat. Optional ingredients may improve texture, extend shelf life, or stop syneresis, which is liquid separating out. A flavoring that characterizes the product is declared with the name.

entries.question: How do you tell real ice cream from a lookalike?

entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 135.110, ice cream holds at least 10 percent milkfat and at least 4.5 pounds to the gallon. The pounds-per-gallon floor limits how much air is whipped in. A carton with neither claim ranks last: US rules let rBST use go unlabeled.

entries.short_answer: Clarified butter is butter simmered until the water is gone and the fat separates from the milk solids. The solids are removed. Ghee simmers longer, which gives it a nutty taste.
entries.detail: Ghee is typically made by simmering butter, skimming the surface, and keeping the clear liquid fat. The solid residue that settles is discarded. Clarified butter is done once the water evaporates and the fat separates from the milk solids. Ghee is simmered further, which makes it nutty and aromatic. Spices can be added for flavor. Its smoke point, the heat where the fat starts to break down, is 250 °C (482 °F).

entries.title: Goat and sheep dairy
entries.question: How do you pick goat or sheep dairy?
entries.decision: Plain whole goat or sheep milk, nothing else added.
entries.why: Goat milk has less lactose than cow’s milk.
entries.short_answer: Goat milk averages about 3.5 percent butterfat. It contains lactose, less than cow’s milk. Goat butter is white. Popular sheep cheeses include feta, pecorino romano, Roquefort and Manchego.
entries.detail: Goat milk generally averages 3.5 percent butterfat. Its fat globules are small and well emulsified, so the cream stays suspended longer than in cow’s milk. Its cream rises over a few days. Compared with cow’s milk, goat milk has less lactose and different forms of proteins. Goat milk is made into cheese, butter, ice cream and yogurt. In France, goat cheese is called fromage de chèvre. Goat butter is white because goats convert yellow beta-carotene to a colorless form of vitamin A. entries.title: The dairy case
entries.question: How do you choose dairy at the store?
entries.decision: By type: grass-fed, whole, no added vitamins.
entries.why: Each dairy type has its own card. The carton then shows added vitamins, pasture and filtering.
entries.short_answer: Start with the type: milk, yogurt, cheese, butter, cream or a plant drink. Then read the carton. Vitamins A and D are optional in milk, so the label tells. Organic dairy animals must graze pasture.
entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 131.110, adding vitamins A and D to milk is optional. If vitamin D is added, each quart holds 400 International Units (IU), a measure of vitamin amount. Ultrafiltered milk is pushed through a porous membrane under pressure, a process called ultrafiltration. It changes the water, lactose and some minerals, and concentrates the protein already in the milk. The label then shows more protein, less sugar and a longer shelf life.

entries.question: How do you pick kimchi?
entries.decision: Raw kimchi, fermented with salt, refrigerated in glass.

entries.short_answer: Read the list for cabbage, red pepper powder, garlic, ginger and salt, and for fish sauce or shrimp. Check when the kimchi was packed. Fresh kimchi looks crisp, plump and bright. Lighter, softer kimchi is well fermented.
entries.detail: Kimchi is cabbage, usually napa, seasoned with red pepper powder, garlic, ginger and salt (the Codex standard). Fish sauce or salted seafood such as shrimp is often added. Traditional kimchi ferments a few days at room temperature, then moves to cold storage to age for weeks. The packed date shows how long it has fermented, from fresh to ripe to overripe. Ripe kimchi is sour and softer, with some crunch left. Overripe kimchi is intense and juicy, and best cooked into other dishes. Fermenting kimchi makes carbon dioxide gas, so a live jar can be fizzy. Pasteurized or heated kimchi, or a jar soured with vinegar, is no longer a live ferment.

entries.question: How do you find pickles that are actually fermented?
entries.decision: Unheated, salt-brine fermented pickles from the cold case.

entries.detail: Brined pickles sit in salt brine for several weeks. Lactic acid bacteria, the microbes that sour them, make the acid. Quick pickles are made in one or two days by adding vinegar. Pasteurized or heated pickles, and ferments with calcium chloride added, sit on the low rung. Federal rules let acidified foods, meaning foods with acid added, be called pickles. A half-sour has a shorter stay in the brine and is still crisp and bright green. A full-sour is fully fermented. Skip a pickle jar listing sodium benzoate, an added preservative.

entries.detail: A systematic review of ten studies found microplastics in the majority of salt samples, from none detected up to 1,674 particles per kilogram in sea salt, 8 to 462 in lake salt and 0 to 204 in rock and well salt. A study of 39 brands across six continents found that unrefined sea salt tracks the plastic pollution of the seawater around it, unless the particles are filtered out during manufacture. That makes the sea of origin and the way the salt is processed the two things worth reading for. No tested salt type was clear across every sample, so a package promising zero microplastics needs a stated method behind it. Under 21 CFR 100.155, table salt with no added iodide must carry a statement that it “does not supply iodide” right after the name. An anticaking agent, an additive that keeps salt from caking, may be added under 21 CFR 172.490, and the list names it. Sea salt is made by evaporating seawater and usually has larger crystals than the fine grains of table salt. Flaked salt is a type of sea salt with larger, irregular flakes. Pickling or canning salt is pure salt with nothing added, and it keeps a brine clear. Kosher salt has a coarse texture, so salts do not swap cup for cup. Pink Himalayan salt is sodium chloride, like other salts. Curing salt, sometimes dyed pink and labeled “pink salt,” is a different product used for curing meats.

entries.title: Vinegar
entries.question: How do you pick vinegar?
entries.decision: Organic raw cider, wine or balsamic vinegar, not distilled white.
entries.why: WAPF avoid list names distilled vinegar.
entries.short_answer: Read the percent acidity on the label. Canning and pickling recipes use 5 percent, and 4 percent bottles are sold too. Vinegar keeps almost indefinitely; best-by is about quality. On balsamic, only the full protected names carry aging rules.
entries.detail: Vinegar labels state percent acidity. Some state grain instead, a strength unit where 10 grain equals 1 percent acidity, so 50 grain is 5 percent. The acid in vinegar is acetic acid; as an ingredient, acetic acid is produced by fermentation or by synthesis. Once a bottle is open, harmless vinegar bacteria can cloud it, and a mother, a soft floating mass, can form when pasteurization was incomplete; both are harmless. Traditionally, wine vinegar was made the slow way: in the Orleans process, wood barrels of fermented alcohol liquid acetify for about 1 to 3 months. Most vinegar is now made from distilled grain alcohol, and the most common method today is the faster submerged method. As Il Post reports, the words aceto and balsamico on their own are generic; only the full protected names carry a rule. Traditional Balsamic Vinegar of Modena (DOP) is made from cooked grape must and aged in wooden barrels for at least 12 years, and at least 25 for Extravecchio. Aceto Balsamico di Modena (IGP) is cooked or concentrated grape must, at least 20 percent of the starting mass, with wine vinegar added, aged at least 60 days in wood under the Emilia-Romagna IGP rules.

entries.title: Jam and preserves
entries.question: How do you pick jam or preserves?
entries.decision: Organic fruit jam sweetened with honey or maple syrup.
entries.why: Traditional guides pick organic jam with a natural sweetener and no added acids. Jelly is strained juice.
entries.short_answer: Look for “Jam” or “Preserves” in the name. Both are standardized and made from fruit with sugar. Jelly is made from strained juice. Reduced-sugar jars keep a shorter time once opened, so refrigerate them.
entries.detail: “Jam” and “Preserves” are standardized names. Jam is made from fruit and sugar at a fixed ratio: at least 47 parts fruit to 55 parts sugar for some fruits, and 45 to 55 for the rest. The finished jam is cooked to not less than 65 percent soluble solids. Jelly is made from the filtered or strained juice of the fruit. Pectin is the natural substance in fruit that makes it gel; commercial pectins are made from apples or citrus fruit. Special pectins exist for jars with less sugar or no added sugar. Those jars do not use sugar as a preservative, so some require refrigeration. When a jam names several fruits, they are listed in order of predominance. Sugar can weigh more than the fruit in a standard jam. By one extension definition, jam is a sweet spread that holds its shape, made from crushed or chopped fruit. Jelly is a firm gel made from juice. Preserves are small whole fruits or uniform pieces in a thick, gelled syrup. Home-kitchen (cottage-food) jam follows the same federal standard of identity for each product.

entries.detail: Ketchup’s federal standard, 21 CFR 155.194, accepts three names: catsup, ketchup or catchup. It starts from tomato concentrate or liquid from red tomatoes. Vinegars, sweeteners, and spices, flavoring, onions or garlic are its optional ingredients. Lemon juice or suitable organic acids may be added only to adjust the pH, a measure of acidity. The mustard description here is the USDA AMS commercial item description, a federal purchase spec rather than retail law. It calls for ground mustard seed, vinegar, turmeric, salt and spices. Yellow seed goes into its Type I and Type II mustards, and brown seed into Types III to IX. Yellow mustard is smooth, with a mild flavor and slight acid taste. Dijon is smooth and pungent, with mild white wine notes. Stone ground is coarse and pungent, with visible specks of mustard seed. Spicy brown is slightly thick. Gums and artificial colors are not permitted, and added water must be declared. As a food history site reports, the Oxford English Dictionary traces ketchup to ke-tsiap. In the Amoy dialect of Chinese, that word means a brine of pickled fish. Mushroom, walnut and fish ketchups stayed more popular in the States until the mid-1800s.

entries.title: Soy sauce and hot sauce
entries.question: How do you pick soy sauce and hot sauce?
entries.decision: Organic naturally brewed soy sauce, labeled raw or unpasteurized.
entries.why: Traditional soy sauce ferments for months; a fast acid method takes hours. Wheat and gluten-free are label facts.
entries.short_answer: Traditionally brewed soy sauce ferments for months. A fast method makes it with acid in hours. Shoyu is about equal wheat and soybeans; tamari is mostly soybeans. Some fermented hot sauces have no added vinegar.
entries.detail: Classic soy sauce is made by microbial fermentation. Soybeans and wheat are inoculated with Aspergillus oryzae, a mold. Traditional soy sauce then ferments for months or even a year. A fast method makes hydrolyzed soy protein with acid in hours, called acid hydrolysis. A USDA AMS purchase description covers both methods; it is a federal buying spec, not retail label law. It names Type I, fermented, made from koji: wheat and soybeans cultured with Aspergillus oryzae. It names Type II, non-fermented, a blend made from hydrolyzed vegetable protein. Shoyu, the prevalent Japanese style, is made from roughly equal parts wheat and soybeans. Tamari is described as all or mostly soybeans, with no wheat. As TASTE reports, tamari began in Japan as a by-product of miso making. Liquid pooled at the bottom of the miso barrel, and it was used for seasoning. Wheat is a gluten-containing grain. A gluten-free claim means any unavoidable gluten is below 20 ppm, or 20 mg per kilogram of food. A hot sauce cooked with vinegar may fall under the rules for acidified foods. A fermented hot sauce with no added vinegar may follow a different review process. Traditionally, hot pepper sauce is made from a salted pepper mash aged in barrels, and one study aged it in oak.

entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 101.61, sodium words on a label have set meanings per standard serving. Sodium free means less than 5 mg. Very low sodium means 35 mg or less. Low sodium means 140 mg or less. Reduced sodium, or less sodium, means at least 25 percent less than a reference food, and the label names that food and the percent difference. Salt is not the same word as sodium; salt means sodium chloride. No salt added means no salt went in during processing, and a soup that is not sodium free says “not a sodium free food”. On the shelf, a slightly dented can is fine, but skip deep dents the size of a finger and dents with sharp points on the seam. Dusty cans or torn labels may mean old stock. Dates on cans mark peak quality, not safety. In a cool, dry pantry, high-acid canned food keeps 12 to 18 months for best quality, and low-acid canned food, including vegetable soups other than tomato, keeps 2 to 5 years.

entries.title: Olives
entries.question: How do you pick olives?
entries.decision: Organic olives labeled naturally brine-fermented and unpasteurized.
entries.why: Fresh olives are bitter, and curing removes it. Brine curing ferments the fruit slowly, with water and salt.
entries.short_answer: Olives off the tree are very bitter, so they are cured before eating. Brine-cured olives ferment slowly in water and salt. Lye-cured olives are a milder style. Opened olives keep about 2 weeks.
entries.detail: Olives picked off the tree hold a very bitter compound called oleuropein. Curing leaches it out. The common curing methods are water, brine, lye and dry salt, and each gives a different texture and flavor. Water-cured olives stay slightly bitter, because water removes less oleuropein. Brine curing is a fermentation that turns the fruit’s sugars into lactic and acetic acids. It uses only water and salt, but takes a long time. Lye curing works quickly, and rinsing leaves a neutral olive that takes on flavors from vinegar and herbs. Salt gives olives their flavor and serves as a preservative. Salt curing has roots in ancient antiquity. Commercial table olives follow three main methods: Greek, Spanish and Californian. Greek-style olives are picked near full ripeness, at the purple stage, and cured in brine. Spanish-style green olives are treated with lye, rinsed, then fermented. California-style black ripe olives are lye-cured and darkened with air, then colored black with an iron salt. One review’s table puts debittering at 6–12 months for Greek, 1–7 months for Spanish and 1 week for California. The California method gives the mildest flavor and the least bitterness. USDA grade standards cover canned ripe olives (U.S. Grade A, B and C). USDA defines green olives as “completely fermented and cured” fruit of the olive tree.

entries.detail: Brown algae are seaweeds of listed species, among them Laminaria, Macrocystis and Undaria species. They are harvested mainly in coastal waters of the northern Atlantic and Pacific. The material is dried and ground or chopped for use in food. Kelp is also used in spices and seasonings as a flavor enhancer. As a food additive, kelp is the dehydrated, ground product made from certain Macrocystis and Laminaria species. One study found the species labeling inadequate or inaccurate for several products. Iodine content varies widely by kind, from 16 µg (micrograms) per gram in nori to over 8165 µg per gram in one sample of processed kelp granules. In Maine, most wild sea vegetables are harvested by hand at low tide in early spring. Harvesters trim the blades and leave the holdfast, the base that anchors the plant, for regrowth. Seaweed harvesting is generally done in the spring and summer months. Bullwhip kelp does not keep well under refrigeration or by freezing, so its blades are dried for storage.

entries.title: Salsa
entries.question: How do you pick a salsa?
entries.decision: Organic fermented salsa, raw or unpasteurized, from the cold case.
entries.why: Fermented salsa is cultured with salt, not heated. A shelf jar is acidified and heat-processed.
entries.short_answer: Salsa mixes onions and peppers with tomatoes. Fermented salsa is cultured with salt and left unheated. A shelf jar is acidified and heat-processed. A fresh tub sold from the cold case stays in the refrigerator.
entries.detail: Most salsa is a mix of low-acid foods, such as onions and peppers, with more acid foods, such as tomatoes. Vinegar or citrus juice, such as lemon or lime, often adds more acid. A shelf jar is an acidified food: acid is added to low-acid ingredients for a pH of 4.6 or below. pH is the measure of acidity. Federal rules also require an acidified food to be thermally processed, that is, heat-processed. Salsas are named among acidified foods. Foods stored, distributed and sold under refrigeration are outside that definition. For a shelf jar sold under inspection, a process authority reviews the recipe and sets its scheduled heat process. Some states have cottage-food laws that let home kitchens sell certain foods without inspection. In Virginia, for example, such a jar sells only directly to shoppers, such as at farmers markets. Its front label states it was processed and prepared without state inspection. Its label also names the maker, physical address and phone number. These are label facts about where a jar was made.

entries.detail: Coconut water is the clear liquid found inside green (unripe) coconuts. Coconut milk is different: it combines the grated meat of a ripe coconut with water. entries.title: Tortilla chips
entries.question: How do you pick tortilla chips?
entries.decision: Organic masa chips fried in coconut oil, lard or ghee.
entries.why: Corn cooked in limewater grinds into masa, a dough. Untreated cornmeal will not form one.
entries.short_answer: Corn for tortillas is cooked in an alkaline solution, usually limewater, then ground into masa. Some corn chips use corn that never went through that step. Masa and a trace of lime often show on the ingredients.
entries.detail: The step is nixtamalization: dry corn is soaked and cooked in a solution of slaked lime and water. Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide, called “cal.” The cooked corn, called nixtamal, is washed, then ground into a dough, masa. The word comes from Nahuatl, the Aztec language. Cornmeal from untreated corn cannot form a dough with water alone. Masa harina means “dough flour,” the powder ground from nixtamal. Masa flour made at scale is based on the traditional method. Restaurant-style chips are tortillas cut into wedges and fried. Most bagged chips are shaped straight from coarse masa dough and fried. For chips, Kristy’s standard is lard, tallow, coconut oil or olive oil. Skip seed oils and avocado oil.

entries.decision: Organic kernels popped at home in butter or coconut oil.
entries.why: Plain kernels pop with no oil at all, so the cook decides on any butter, oil or salt.
entries.short_answer: Popcorn is its own variety of corn. Water inside the hard hull turns to steam, the hull bursts and the kernel turns inside out. Plain kernels pop in a paper bag in the microwave, no oil needed.
entries.detail: Popcorn is a variety of corn, Zea mays everta. Its hard outer hull is the pericarp. Inside, moisture runs about 13 to 14.5 percent of the kernel. As the water heats, the kernel acts as a pressure cooker until the hull ruptures. Kernels with cuts or weak spots in the hull let the moisture escape and stay unpopped. In one study, 4 to 47 percent of kernels failed to pop, depending on variety. Two popped shapes are grown, butterfly and mushroom. Mushroom popcorn is often sold prepopped and coated with flavorings. For popping at home, Kristy’s standard is coconut oil, butter or tallow. Skip seed oils and avocado oil.

entries.short_answer: Traditional German pretzels are dipped in a diluted, food-grade lye bath, then baked. Baking neutralizes the lye. The bath gives the chew and the glossy brown crust. A baking soda bath does the same job, milder.
entries.detail: Lye is sodium hydroxide, the strongest alkali a baker uses. On the pH scale, a measure of how strong an alkali is, lye reaches 14. The alkaline surface speeds browning, the Maillard reaction that shapes how the crust forms and tastes. A hard pretzel bakes about twice as long as a soft one. The German name, Laugenbrezel, means “lye pretzel.”
entries.kristy_take: The story goes that monks in the Middle Ages twisted dough scraps into pretzels. German bakers still dip the dough in lye for the deepest color.

entries.detail: Traditionally, Neapolitan dough is made only of flour, water, salt and yeast. The flour is 00 flour, a soft wheat flour of medium strength. The dough rises at least 8 hours, in two phases. Dough balls run 180 to 250 g. They are stretched by hand only, never pressed by machine or rolled with a pin. The finished pizza is no wider than 35 cm. Leftover dough balls are thrown out each evening. The pizza bakes on the floor of a wood oven at 430 to 485°C, for 60 to 90 seconds. The wood must give off no smoke or odor: oak, ash, beech and maple. Well baked means golden and unburnt, with a bread-scented rim and a soft center that folds without breaking. “Verace Pizza Napoletana” is a collective mark, a name its own association governs. It is not a DOP, the Italian protected name given only to first-stage foods such as cheese and oil. Ready pizzas and frozen dough balls are spreading today. On a US label, “pan style” means a pizza marketed in a pan with a thick crust. “Sicilian style” means a thick crust, usually 50 percent or more of the pizza.

entries.title: Frozen fries
entries.question: How do you pick frozen fries?
entries.decision: Organic frozen fries cooked in tallow, lard or coconut oil.
entries.why: At home, a hash brown takes potatoes, oil, salt and pepper. The bag’s list shows what else is in it.
entries.short_answer: Read the ingredient list on the bag. At home, a hash brown takes potatoes, oil, salt and pepper. Home fries take starchy potatoes and salt. Compare bags by what they list beyond those.
entries.detail: The federal grade standard describes frozen french fries as mature white potatoes, washed, sorted and trimmed. They may be cut or left whole. They are deep-fried or blanched in fat or oil, then frozen. Blanching is a short cook in hot water or steam. In a plant, the strips are peeled, cut and blanched, then par-fried, meaning partly fried, and frozen. Blanching also leaches sugars from the strips. The fries are finish-fried from frozen to develop color and crispness. Why it works: frying is first a dehydration process, meaning it drives water out of the food. The drier the food going in, the better the crust. So cooks fry once, freeze, and fry again. As food cools, moisture moves from the center to the surface. The second fry boils it off. The first fry also leaves simpler pathways inside, so water escapes more easily the second time. An air fryer is a convection appliance, meaning it circulates hot air. It cooks faster than an oven and gives a crisp outside. French fries cook well in one. For added fat, Kristy’s standard is tallow, olive oil, or coconut oil. Skip seed oils and avocado oil. Look for thick-cut fries on the bag. Acrylamide forms during high-heat browning; it is a cooking byproduct, not an added ingredient.

entries.title: Frozen
entries.question: How do you shop the frozen aisle?
entries.decision: Organic frozen fruit and vegetables with the food alone listed.
entries.why: Food held at 0°F or below keeps its color, flavor and texture better than warmer food.
entries.short_answer: Most frozen fruit and vegetables are frozen piece by piece, quickly. A plain bag lists the produce alone. A bag frozen into one solid block has likely thawed and refrozen. Packs at the back of the shelf thaw least.
entries.detail: Food stored at 0°F or lower keeps its color, flavor and texture. Food held at 15°F may feel hard, but it is less solidly frozen than at 0°F. Over the same time, the 0°F food holds color, flavor and texture better. Freezing keeps quality but cannot improve flavor or texture. Processors flash-freeze food, which means freezing it very fast. Sellers keep it at 0°F or below to hold quality. Fast freezing makes tiny ice crystals. Slow freezing makes large ones that rupture cells, so moisture leaks out on thawing. Freezer burn shows as grayish-brown leathery spots where air reached the food. It can also show as white, dried-out patches that turn tough and dry. Folded foil can develop pinholes that let freezer burn in. Store shrink-film on meat breathes, so overwrap it to stop freezer burn. Freezer times and dates on frozen food mark quality only. “Do not refreeze” on a package is the packer’s quality advice. Quality can drop, and the packer cannot know home thawing conditions. Vermont’s rule has frozen display cases hold air at 0°F or lower. Each case there has a thermometer. A load line marks the top of the cold air at each end of the case. Cases sit away from door drafts, fans, lights and heaters. Thaw in the fridge, in cold water or in the microwave. Cooking from frozen takes about one and a half times as long.

entries.title: Baby food
entries.question: Which baby food should I buy?
entries.decision: Single-food purees and infant oatmeal, not rice snacks.
entries.why: Rice-based snacks and rice cereal test highest for arsenic in baby food studies.
entries.short_answer: Testing found heavy metals in most baby foods, store-bought and homemade alike. Rice cakes, crisped rice cereal and rice puffs ran highest. A varied rotation is the main step.
entries.detail: Healthy Babies Bright Futures tested baby foods for lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium. Homemade purees carried detectable metals as often as store-bought ones. The most contaminated foods were rice cakes, crisped rice cereal, rice-based puffs, brown rice and teething biscuits. Among the least were banana, grits, plain meats, butternut squash, apple, eggs and watermelon. Four of seven infant rice cereals exceeded FDA’s proposed action level for inorganic arsenic. Their swaps are infant oatmeal for rice cereal, fresh or frozen fruit for canned, and peeled sweet potatoes.

buying_tips: Read for ‘nixtamalized’ or ‘corn treated with lime’: corn soaked in limewater.
Look for ‘organic’ on the bag.
Check the frying fat: coconut oil, lard from pastured pigs, or ghee.
Skip oil blends, flavor powders, artificial colors and preservatives.

entries.title: Sliced-potato chips
entries.decision: Potato chips fried in coconut oil, lard or ghee.
entries.why: Sliced potatoes differ from crisps formed from flakes and starch. Accepted fats include sourced lard or tallow, coconut or olive oil. These are formula preferences, without a universal ranking of animal fat over coconut oil.
buying_tips: Read the oil: coconut oil, lard from pastured pigs, or ghee.
Look for ‘USDA Organic’ on the front of the bag.
Pick plain salted with the shortest list.
Skip partially hydrogenated oil, unnamed oil blends and flavorings.

sources.name: Traditional cooking and finishing fat preferences

entries.title: Frozen potato fries
entries.decision: Fries of potatoes alone, or potatoes cooked in tallow or lard.
entries.why: Tallow, sourced lard and coconut oil fit the lead preference, with olive oil or no added oil also accepted. A potato-only retail option must be confirmed on an actual pack. Oven or air-fryer directions do not change the oil already in the product.
buying_tips: Read the list: potatoes, plus tallow (beef fat) or lard and salt at most.
Read every oil, including the coating and seasoning.
Look for ‘USDA Organic’ with potatoes listed first.
Skip vegetable-oil blends, sugar and starch coatings.

sources.name: Traditional cooking and finishing fat preferences

entries.title: Cooking fats and simple spreads
entries.decision: One fat on its own: extra virgin olive oil, virgin coconut oil, butter or lard.
entries.why: Olive, coconut, dairy and rendered animal fats need different source and use checks. A plant spread qualifies only if its entire formula passes; no qualifying retail spread is assumed available.
buying_tips: Look for one named fat on the label, not a blend.
Skip bottles that say only ‘vegetable oil’.
Pick dark glass or tin with a harvest date over clear bottles.
Skip margarine, shortening and partially hydrogenated oils.

entries.title: Named-source sweeteners
entries.decision: One sweetener on its own: raw honey, pure maple syrup, molasses or coconut sugar.
entries.why: Honey, maple syrup, coconut sugar, whole-cane juice and molasses have distinct production methods. Raw is a honey-specific preference; heating is part of making other sweeteners. Local or regional traceability is preferred where the crop exists, without implying a health advantage.
buying_tips: Read the list: one sweetener alone, nothing mixed in.
Look for ‘raw’ on honey and ‘pure’ on maple syrup, plus USDA Organic.
Pick honey, maple, molasses or coconut sugar over white sugar.
Skip corn syrup, brown rice syrup, agave and imitation syrups.

entries.title: Plain fruit preparations
entries.decision: Fruit with nothing added: dried fruit, applesauce, coconut water.
entries.why: Dried fruit, cooked applesauce and coconut water do not share one processing standard. Read the complete formula for sweeteners, coatings and preservation additions. Prefer disclosed fruit and maker sources where available; plain water is a narrow applesauce fallback.
buying_tips: Read the list: the fruit alone, or fruit and water.
Skip added sugar, syrup, juice concentrate, oil coating and sulfites.
Look for USDA Organic on the bag, jar or carton.

Look for ‘USDA Organic’ on the pack or the bin label.
Pick sealed packs for nuts, flour and brown rice; bins suit beans and lentils.
Look for ‘BPA-free lining’ on cans.

entries.title: Bread and bakery
entries.decision: Sourdough or sprouted bread with whole grain listed first.
buying_tips: Read the first ingredient for ‘whole’; ‘enriched’ means white flour.
Look for the 100% Whole Grain Stamp, not the 50%+ or Basic one.

entries.title: Snacks
entries.decision: Whole nuts, fruit or popcorn first; packaged snacks with a short list of real food.

Read the frying oil by name; skip partially hydrogenated oil.
Check that crackers list a whole grain first.
Skip packs with flavor packets, natural flavors, added syrups, artificial colors or unnamed oils.
Can’t find whole nuts, fruit or kernels? Pick the packaged snack with the shortest list of real food.

entries.title: Fermented soy foods
entries.decision: Miso, tempeh and other soy foods that are naturally fermented, short list.
entries.why: Miso, tempeh and natto use different cultures and recipes. Fermentation does not establish ready-to-eat status, and pasteurization does not erase fermentation. Prefer a label with useful origin and batch details.
buying_tips: Look for ‘naturally fermented’ or ‘traditionally brewed’ on the pack.
Read the list: whole soybeans, named grains, salt and cultures.
Pick packs that say where the beans were grown.
Skip hydrolyzed soy protein, caramel color and flavorings, sauce packets included.

entries.title: Vinegar: source, process and acidity
entries.decision: Raw, unfiltered vinegar ‘with the mother’, from a named fruit or wine.
entries.why: Raw table vinegar and traditionally aged balsamic are separate culinary choices. Balsamic begins with cooked grape must, so a never-heated rule cannot cover both. Prefer a maker that discloses orchard or barrel details.
buying_tips: Look for ‘raw’, ‘unfiltered’ and ‘with the mother’ on the bottle.
Look for USDA Organic and one named fruit or wine on the list.
Skip distilled vinegar and bottles that list caramel or natural flavors.

entries.title: Bone-broth bases and soups
entries.decision: Bone broth with bones on the list, no yeast extract or flavor powder.
entries.why: Prefer home stock or a small maker disclosing pasture-raised poultry or pork and 100% grass-fed beef. Water can lead the ingredient list, and frozen cubes can be actual concentrated stock. A cold gel or container format does not establish the animal source or recipe.
buying_tips: Read the list for bones and which animal they came from.
Look for USDA Organic; ‘pasture-raised’ or ‘100% grass-fed’ bones are better.
Pick short lists: broth, meat, vegetables, herbs and salt.
Skip yeast extract, MSG, hydrolyzed protein and flavor powders.

entries.title: Vegetable and seed condiments
entries.decision: Sauce with vegetables first, a short list and no added sugar.
entries.why: Tomato sauce and salsa share a vegetable base, with different cooked, fresh or fermented formats. Prefer seasonal local vegetables or a small maker with harvest and recipe details. Preserved ripe-season tomatoes are a practical alternative outside the harvest.
buying_tips: Read the first ingredient: tomatoes or the named vegetable.
Look for ‘USDA Organic’ on the jar.
Pick glass jars, or cans marked ‘BPA-free’, for tomatoes.
Skip sugar, corn syrup, citric acid and ‘natural flavors’ on the list.

entries.title: Olive-oil pesto
entries.decision: Pesto made with extra virgin olive oil as the only oil.
entries.why: Traditional pesto combines basil, pine nuts, aged cheese, garlic and salt with olive oil. Named nut, seed or cheese-free variations can qualify without matching that exact recipe. Prefer a small maker with clear process and source details.
buying_tips: Read the oil: extra virgin olive oil and no other.
Skip sunflower, canola or soybean oil, starch and added flavors.
Check that every herb, nut, seed and cheese is named.
Look for ‘organic’ on the jar.

entries.title: Mayonnaise: disclosed oils
entries.decision: Mayonnaise made with olive oil only and pasture-raised eggs.
entries.why: The full oil blend matters more than the front label. Olive oil leads this preference; skip avocado oil. Prefer a small maker disclosing ingredients and egg sourcing.
buying_tips: Read the whole oil list: olive oil and nothing else.
Skip jars that add soybean, canola or ‘vegetable oil’ next to olive oil.
Look for ‘pasture-raised’ eggs on the jar.
Pick jars that say where the eggs come from.

entries.title: Olive-oil or cultured-dairy dressings and salads
entries.decision: Dressings and deli salads made with extra virgin olive oil or plain yogurt.
entries.why: Creamy dressing can use cultured dairy without added oil. Any mayonnaise or premixed dressing brings its own ingredient list and oil check. Prefer a small maker’s disclosed recipe or home assembly with seasonal vegetables and herbs.
buying_tips: Read every oil, including the mayo or dressing inside a salad.
Pick extra virgin olive oil, or plain yogurt or sour cream, as the base.
Skip soybean, canola, corn or unnamed oils, EDTA and added flavors.
Look for ‘organic’ on the tub or bottle.

entries.title: Dry seasonings and infusions
entries.decision: Organic herbs, spices and tea with nothing added and no radiation treatment.
entries.why: Whole spices, dried herbs and tea need different form and freshness checks. Prefer a small grower or direct source with origin and harvest or batch details. Steam processing is distinct from irradiation or chemical fumigation.
buying_tips: Look for USDA Organic on herbs, spices, tea and coffee.
Check for ‘Treated with radiation’ or the irradiation logo, and skip it.
Read the list: the plant alone, no fillers, flavors or anti-caking agents.
Skip spices, herbs and seaweed marked ‘Product of China’.

entries.title: Occasional cocoa foods
entries.decision: Cocoa or chocolate with a short list and where the cacao grew printed.
entries.why: Plain powder and eating chocolate have different sweetener rules. Prefer a small producer with origin and process disclosure. Cocoa percentage, organic status and source stories do not establish a batch’s metal levels.
buying_tips: Read the list: cocoa or cacao first, little else.
Skip lecithin, flavorings, other fats, and bars with sugar listed first.
Look for Regenerative Organic Certified; ‘organic’ is next.
Look for lead and cadmium test results dated for the same batch.

entries.title: Sweet bakery: flour, fat and sweetener

entries.why: Prefer soaked or sprouted whole-grain baking made at home or by a small maker. Whole-grain muffins with those fats and sweeteners are the fallback. Laminated pastry has a separate occasional unbleached-flour, all-butter route; it does not meet the prepared-whole-grain preference.
buying_tips: Look for whole-grain flour and ‘sprouted’ or ‘sourdough’ on the pack.
Read the fat: butter or coconut oil.

Look for USDA Organic and the fruit named beside ‘Jam’ or ‘Preserves’.

buying_tips: Look for ‘fermented’, ‘live’ or ‘unpasteurized’ on the bottle.
Look for ‘USDA Organic’.

Skip syrup, added sugar, flavorings and puffed cereal.

entries.title: Wild-first seafood
entries.decision: Wild-caught fish, with the kind of fish and where it was caught on the label.
entries.why: Species, harvest origin and additions establish what is being purchased. Small seasonal fisheries lead this sourcing preference, while prompt freezing can retain catch quality beyond the season. Wild sourcing is an editorial preference and does not establish the absence of processing additions.
buying_tips: Read the label for ‘wild-caught’, the kind of fish and where it was caught.
Look for the blue MSC logo; it means an outside group checked the fishery.
Read the list: just the fish, salt at most.

entries.title: Trout: wild first, conditional farmed fallback
entries.decision: Wild trout when sold; otherwise US farm-raised rainbow trout.
entries.why: The current trout card permits a farmed fallback, while the traditional selection source rejects farmed trout. A disclosed trout ration can contain plant proteins, oils and pigment despite spring-fed wording. This separate conditional route preserves the item distinction without making domestic origin or an environmental rating a feed guarantee.
buying_tips: Look for ‘wild-caught’ trout and where it was caught.
Pick US farm-raised rainbow trout next; read ‘farm-raised’ and the country.
Look for the ASC logo on farmed trout; an outside group checks the farm.
Skip trout labeled ‘color added’.

entries.title: Tinned fish: species and packing medium
entries.decision: Wild fish in a tin, plain or in water or olive oil, with a short list.
entries.why: Species, packing medium and recipe are separate label checks. Traceable seasonal catch and a short suitable recipe lead this preference, with a clearly labeled plain tin as the fallback. Skin and edible bones are form preferences for particular fish, not a requirement for every tin.
buying_tips: Read the tin for ‘wild’, the kind of fish and where it was caught.
Read the list: fish, plus water or olive oil and salt at most.
Skip tins that list soy oil, sunflower oil or hydrolyzed protein.
Check the tin has no bulges, leaks or dented seams.

entries.title: Crab and lobster: live, cooked or frozen
entries.decision: Crab or lobster with the kind and where it was caught named; moving if live.
entries.why: Movement applies to animals sold live, while cooked portions and frozen meat need their own condition checks. Small seasonal fisheries lead the sourcing preference, with plain cooked or frozen formats as alternatives. A whole live animal is a form preference, not an established nutritional advantage over properly frozen meat.
buying_tips: Read the tag for the kind and where it was caught.
Check that live ones move their legs or claws.
Look for the MSC logo on frozen or cooked crab and lobster.
Pick plain frozen or cooked if no live ones are there; read ‘raw’ or ‘cooked’.

entries.title: Tagged live bivalves
entries.decision: Live clams, mussels or oysters with a harvest tag and whole shells.
entries.why: Harvest water, date and shipper details identify a live shellfish lot. Marine-farmed bivalves can qualify, so a wild-first finfish preference does not transfer to this family. Growing systems differ: marine plankton feeding does not establish that every farm receives no added food.
buying_tips: Ask the fish counter to see the harvest tag on loose shellfish.
Read the tag for the water they came from and the harvest date.
Check oysters, mussels and hard clams: whole shells that close when tapped.
Pick farmed mussels and oysters as gladly as wild; both rate top.

entries.title: Dry-packed scallops
entries.decision: Dry-packed scallops, with scallops the only ingredient.
entries.why: Dry-packed wording alone does not establish the soaking history. Documented short-trip catch leads the preference, and promptly frozen catch can retain that source off-season. Added water and phosphate are processing distinctions here, without a toxicity claim.
buying_tips: Read ‘dry’ or ‘dry-packed’ on the pack or the counter sign.
Read the list: scallops only, no added water or phosphates.
Ask the fish counter whether the scallops are dry or wet-packed (soaked).
Pick frozen dry scallops if the counter has only wet ones.

entries.title: Cured seafood: method and format
entries.decision: Wild smoked fish or roe, kind of fish named, cured with salt and wood smoke.
entries.why: Species, curing and required storage matter more than traditional or artisan wording. Salt-cured, smoked and pasteurized formats differ, so neither raw status nor smoking is universal. Preserved seasonal catch can qualify without a shared raw-over-heated health ranking.
buying_tips: Read for ‘wild-caught’, the kind of fish and where it was caught.
Skip liquid smoke, smoke flavoring and added colors on the list.
Check the label for how it was cured and how to store it.
Pick packs kept cold or frozen, as the label says.

entries.title: Seafood

Look for the blue MSC logo on wild fish and the ASC logo on farmed: an outside group checked both.

Read the list: the food alone; skip citric acid, ascorbic acid and sugar.

entries.title: Bottled water
entries.decision: Spring or mineral water in glass or cans, nothing added.
entries.why: Spring and mineral water are defined by an underground source; distilled and treated-tap water are defined by a treatment. Glass bottles or cans, with no sweeteners or flavorings, are the traditional pick.
buying_tips: Read the name: ‘spring’ or ‘mineral’ means it comes from underground.
Check for ‘distilled’ or ‘municipal source’; that is treated water, not a spring.
Pick glass bottles or cans over plastic.
Skip waters with added sweeteners or flavors.

entries.decision: Read the sticker and the sign: organic code, wax and where it grew.
buying_tips: Read the sticker: 5 digits starting with 9 is organic; 4 digits is conventional.
Look for USDA Organic; Real Organic or Certified Naturally Grown go further.
Read the sign for ‘coated with’ to see what wax is on the skin.
Check the sign or sticker for ‘Product of’ to see where it grew.
entries.title: Produce signs and stickers
entries.why: Most of what a produce shelf tells a shopper is printed on the PLU sticker, the bin sign and the seal. The PLU system is voluntary, so the USDA Organic seal or an organic sign is the firmer check. Real Organic Project certifies soil-grown organic crops; Certified Naturally Grown is a peer-review certification without synthetic chemicals or GMOs. Coated fruit must be disclosed as waxed or coated, and country of origin must be on a sign, sticker, band or tag.

entries.decision: Plain frozen fruit or vegetables, with no syrup or sauce.
buying_tips: Read the list for syrup on fruit and sauce on vegetables; skip both.
Look for USDA Organic on the front of the bag.
entries.title: Frozen plain fruit and vegetables
entries.why: Plain frozen produce is a good pick in any season. Freezing slows ripening enzymes rather than stopping them, so blanched, quick-frozen pieces hold best. A bag frozen into one block or thick with frost has likely thawed and refrozen. Some frozen fruit comes in syrup and some vegetables come sauced, so the ingredient list is the check.

entries.title: Molasses
entries.decision: Pure molasses, listed first, before any other sweetener.

entries.title: Date and coconut sugar
entries.decision: Date or coconut sweetener, with the date or coconut named on the bag.

entries.title: Refined syrups
entries.decision: Skip corn syrup, agave and brown rice syrup; pick pure maple syrup instead.

entries.title: Nuts and seeds
entries.decision: Raw nuts and seeds in a sealed pack, only the nut or seed listed.

entries.title: Canned vegetables and fish
entries.decision: Cans marked ‘BPA-free lining’, holding plain foods and little else.

entries.title: Jarred vegetable sauces
entries.decision: Jarred sauce with vegetables first and the oil, salt and spices each named.

entries.title: Soy sauce
entries.decision: Soy sauce that says ‘naturally fermented’ or ‘brewed’ on the bottle.

entries.title: Breakfast cereal
entries.decision: Skip cereal pressed into puffs, loops or shapes; pick whole-grain hot cereal.
